overview.summary: Japan is a chain of islands off the east coast of Asia, where a long-isolated island culture repeatedly absorbed ideas from abroad and made them its own. In just a few decades after 1868 it went from a feudal shogunate to an industrial power.
languages: Japanese — the national language (no law formally designates an official language)
Ainu and Ryukyuan languages are Indigenous to Hokkaido and Okinawa
overview.government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; the emperor is a symbol of the state
geography: Four main islands — Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku — plus thousands of smaller ones
Mostly mountainous and volcanic; Mount Fuji (3,776 m) is the highest peak
Sits where several tectonic plates meet, so earthquakes and tsunamis are a constant risk
overview.climate: Ranges from snowy, cold winters in Hokkaido to subtropical Okinawa; most of the country has four distinct seasons and a rainy season in early summer.
culture: Shinto and Buddhism coexist, and many people take part in the customs of both
Kyoto was the imperial capital for over a thousand years and keeps many temples, shrines and gardens
Seasonal traditions such as viewing cherry blossoms (hanami) are woven into daily life

history.title: The Jōmon: hunter-gatherers who made pottery
history.text: The Jōmon culture is named after the cord-marked patterns on its pottery, some of the oldest in the world. Jōmon people lived mostly by hunting, fishing and gathering for thousands of years.
history.note: Start and end dates differ between scholars and regions.

history.title: Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor
history.text: Japan's 8th-century chronicles say the first emperor, Jimmu, took the throne in 660 BCE. Historians treat Jimmu as a legendary figure; the date was calculated much later and does not match archaeological evidence.

history.title: The Yayoi: rice and metal arrive
history.text: Wet-rice farming, bronze and iron spread into Japan from the Asian mainland, transforming society. Villages grew larger and local rulers emerged.
history.note: Radiocarbon studies suggest rice farming may have begun several centuries earlier than the traditional c. 300 BCE.

history.title: Nara becomes the first permanent capital
history.text: Modelled on Chang'an, the capital of Tang China, Nara (Heijō-kyō) became Japan's capital in 710. Great Buddhist temples such as Tōdai-ji rose there.

history.title: The Heian period: Kyoto's golden age
history.text: The capital moved to Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794. Court culture flourished: Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji, written in the early 11th century, is often called the world's first novel.

history.title: The Kamakura shogunate
history.text: After defeating the rival Taira clan, Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a military government in Kamakura. Real power passed from the imperial court to the shōgun and his samurai, a system that lasted in some form until 1868.
history.note: Historians date its start to 1185 (Yoritomo's victory) or 1192 (when he received the title of shōgun).

history.title: The Mongol invasions
history.text: Kublai Khan's forces twice attacked Kyushu. Both invasions failed, helped by storms later remembered as kamikaze, "divine winds".

history.title: The Sengoku 'Warring States' period
history.text: Central authority collapsed and rival warlords (daimyō) fought for control. Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi reunified the country by 1590.

history.title: The Tokugawa shogunate and 250 years of peace
history.text: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603 and ruled from Edo (modern Tokyo). The shogunate strictly limited foreign trade and contact, and Japan enjoyed a long era of internal peace in which cities, arts and commerce flourished.

history.title: The Meiji Restoration
history.text: The shogunate fell and power returned to the emperor. Japan rapidly modernised its army, industry, schools and government, borrowing ideas from Europe and America.

history.title: Hiroshima, Nagasaki and surrender
history.text: After years of war across Asia and the Pacific, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August). Japan announced its surrender on 15 August.

history.title: A new constitution and the economic miracle
history.text: Japan's postwar constitution took effect in 1947, renouncing war as a sovereign right. Within decades the country became one of the world's largest economies.

places.name: Himeji Castle
places.summary: The 'White Heron Castle', the finest surviving example of early 17th-century Japanese castle building.
details: Himeji-jo's white-plastered walls and layered roofs make it the most celebrated of Japan's original castles, completed in the early 1600s.

places.name: Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
places.summary: Seventeen temples, shrines and a castle from Japan's imperial capital of over a thousand years.
details: Built in 794 on the model of Chinese capitals, Kyoto was Japan's imperial capital until the 19th century. The listing includes famous sites such as Kiyomizu-dera, Kinkaku-ji and Nijō Castle.

places.name: Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
places.type: Temples & palace site · UNESCO World Heritage
places.summary: Japan's 8th-century capital, home of Tōdai-ji and its giant bronze Buddha.
details: Nara's temples and shrines, and the remains of the Heijō Palace, show how Chinese and Korean influences shaped early Japanese culture.

places.name: Itsukushima Shinto Shrine
places.summary: The 'floating' torii gate of Miyajima, which appears to stand on the sea at high tide.
details: The shrine buildings were designed to sit over the water, set against the forested mountain of Miyajima island.

places.name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome)
places.summary: The ruined building that stood closest to the first atomic bomb attack and survived.
details: The dome was left as it was after the bombing of 6 August 1945, as a symbol of the destructive force of nuclear weapons and of hope for peace.

places.name: Mount Fuji (Fujisan)
places.summary: Japan's highest peak, a place of pilgrimage and a lasting inspiration for artists.
details: Fujisan is listed as a cultural site: a sacred place of worship and pilgrimage, and the subject of countless works of art, including Hokusai's prints.
